14242-the-touchstone-of-fortune-being-th:
Charles Major's 1912 memoir novel follows Baron Clyde through the doleful reign of Charles II, the so-called Merry Monarch. Fortune, the narrator argues, smiles on a man who risks all on a desperate chance: losers look foolish, winners look lucky, but courage mints the coin. George Hamilton, penniless second son of a great house, supplies the proof.

Court scandal drives the plot. Frances and Nelly visit the Old Swan, where grilled lobster draws the narrator for lunch, and a maid's innocent tale to the king brings trouble to Frances and George. Secrecy becomes the only shield: Sarah suggests testifying that her sister stayed home since yesterday noon, with father and John Churchill to swear it. Charles Major writes Restoration intrigue with relish, and fortune's touchstone tests every character it meets.
38282-the-herriges-horror-in-philadelphi:
Herriges Horror in Philadelphia is a pamphlet history of a cruelty case in that city. Its full title calls it a full history of the whole affair for the reader. A man, it says, was kept in a dark cage like a wild beast for twenty years, as alleged. The cage stood in his own mother and brother house, the title alleges of the case.

The most fiendish cruelty of the century is the pamphlet verdict on its own story in its heads. Such pamphlets were sold on the street at the height of a scandal trial in the city. The Herriges case, of a son caged by his family, fed the Philadelphia papers and the penny press together. The pamphlet is a specimen of the horror literature of the American city, half report and half sermon, printed while the court still sat on the facts it retails.
47161-the-mad-pranks-of-tom-tram-son-in-:
A Glasgow press printed this chapbook of jests in the year 1802. Its full head names the mad pranks of Tom Tram, son-in-law to Mother Winter. To them are added his merry jests, odd fancies, and sweet tales, said to be most sweet to read. The first part tells a jest twixt old Mother Winter and Tom. She had but one son-in-law, and his name was Tom.

Tom was a grown man, yet he would do no work but what he liked. That fact grieved his mother-in-law to the heart. One day at the mart she heard a call made by the town. All men who would not work were to be whipped. She leapt for joy and ran home to tell her son. His reply is the jest: he gives the mayor his thanks, for his part he will not break the rule.
47808-dog-breaking-the-most-expeditious-:
Hutchinson, a former colonel of the Grenadier Guards, wrote Dog Breaking as a training manual for sporting dogs. John Murray of London published this fourth edition, revised and enlarged, in 1865. The subtitle promises the most expeditious, certain, and easy method. It serves readers who want great excellence or only a fair standard.

The preface speaks with dry humor about a fourth edition. Hutchinson thanks the artist Keyl for fine new sketches. He quotes praise from a stranger to make his case. A keen sportsman had never broken a dog until he found this book a year ago. Pictures of retriever crosses open the volume. The book adds odds and ends for readers who love the dog and gun.
49935-bull-dog-drummond-the-adventures-o:
Sapper, whose real name was Cyril McNeile, wrote Bull-Dog Drummond for Hodder and Stoughton in 1920. Its subtitle calls Drummond a demobilised officer who found peace dull. A prologue opens in December 1918, on the day a British cavalry division marched into Cologne. Flags flew and bands played for the conquerors of a beaten nation. In Berne, the manager of the Hotel Nationale reads a letter twice, puzzled by its contents.

The letter asks for a dinner of four covers, with no expense spared, from an unknown man. Chapters then bring tea at the Carlton, a journey to Godalming, and trouble at Goring. An old game on the Hog's Back, an hour on a roof, and a night in Paris raise the pace. Lakington plays his last coup, and a last round closes the tale.
55814-the-comic-adventures-of-old-mother:
The Comic Adventures of Old Mother Hubbard and Her Dog was printed in London in 1819. Harris and Son issued it at St Paul's Church-yard. Its subtitle boasts the wonderful powers that good old lady possessed in the education of her favourite animal. A portrait of Mother Hubbard, from an original painting, fronts the book. The verses begin with the famous errand. She went to the cupboard to give the poor dog a bone. When she came there, the cupboard was bare.

She goes to the baker's, and the dog is dead; to the undertaker's, and he is laughing. Tripe, beer, wine, fruit, a coat, and a wig follow in turn. The dog smokes a pipe, rides a goat, reads the news, and dances a jig. Dame and dog end with courtesy and bow-wow.
64999-the-golden-harpoon-or-lost-among-t:
The Golden Harpoon, or lost among the floes, is a whaling tale by Roger Starbuck, entered for copyright at New York in 1865. Its contents are short and swift: the golden harpoon, the result, a stove boat, in confinement, and the barricade. Adrift, the chase, and the disappearance carry the middle heads. An unexpected meeting closes the tale as its tenth chapter.

The story opens on the morning of April 25, in a year left blank, on the whale ship Montpelier of New London. She lay at anchor in one of the many bays of the Kamchatka coast, washed by a cold northern sea. As soon as all was made snug below and aloft, the skipper rubbed his hands with pleasure. Even the first mate's face showed a satisfied look, the narrator says.
72100-geological-facts-or-the-crust-of-t:
Geological Facts; or, The Crust of the Earth, What It Is, and What Are Its Uses was written by Barrett, a Dissenting minister of Royston. Arthur Hall, Virtue and Company published the little book in London in 1855. A frontispiece shows the basaltic columns at Regia, in Mexico.

Barrett's preface tells how the book grew. Settled in a quiet Cambridgeshire town, he found young people about him who did not think their education finished when they left school. A geological class was formed, meeting every week, and this manual came out of it. He does not pretend, he says, to teach the science of geology. He aspires simply to give a taste for a noble and elevating study. An epigraph from Sir Thomas Browne's Religio Medici frames the earth as a stair of creatures rising in comely order.
doe-osti-3004239-develop-high-throughput:
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and seqWell, Inc. close CRADA FP00020379 in final report LBNL-2001718, dated October 28, 2025. Nathan Hillson was the lab's technical contact and Jack Leonard the seqWell contact. The project set out to build high-throughput workflows for whole-genome sequencing and insertion site screening. Such screening verifies where engineered DNA actually landed in a microbe's genome, a routine need in biomanufacturing.

Progress was partial, and the report says so plainly. Early phases advanced the sequencing workflow for engineered microbes. A later phase on targeted region pull-down and its data analysis never started: time and resources ran out. The tasks could be reinstated in a future project if interest returns, the authors note. No publications or subject inventions resulted. The Energy Department's bioenergy conversion program sponsored the work, with 50,000 dollars of federal funding.
doe-osti-3005977-develop-high-throughput:
Berkeley Lab's CRADA final report LBNL-2001718, dated October 28, 2025, covers workflow work with seqWell, Inc. under agreement FP00020379. Nathan Hillson was the lab's technical contact and Jack Leonard the company contact. Microbe engineers screening genetic libraries with millions of variants need cheap ways to learn which variant caused a gain. The project aimed to cut the sequencing part of that screening cost threefold while handling more than 1,000 samples per batch.

The team verified that seqWell kits work with the lab's liquid-handling robots and suggested changes to the buffer delivery format for high-throughput runs. A SYBR Green PCR monitoring method was set up so staff can check amplification success and efficiency during runs. Reaction volumes for library preparation were also reduced. DOE funding to the lab was $50,000.
the-touchstone-of-fortune-being-the-memo:
Charles Major's Touchstone of Fortune, dated 1912, purports to be the memoir of Baron Clyde, who lived and fell in the reign of Charles II. The narrator opens with Goddess Fortune, who smiles on men risking everything on a desperate chance; winners, he says, have simply minted their courage. His great example is George Hamilton, penniless younger son of the House of Hamilton, whose elder brother Count Anthony kept an eye on the crumbs from his table.

When Charles II was restored in 1660, Hamilton, who had shared the exile, became Second Gentleman of the Bedchamber at Whitehall. There he lived on pension, card winnings, and disreputable revenues in a court where debts went unpaid and vice was daily jest and pride. Major, author of When Knighthood Was in Flower, writes Restoration intrigue from inside a courtier's cynical memory.
